paragraphs: Katub battora "ki Adonai eloheka mithallek beqereb machaneka vego', vehaya machaneka qadosh velo yireh beka ervat dabar", veqibbelu chaza"l shehu mitzvat aseh shebbekol maqom seAdonai elohenu mithallek immanu dehaynu kesheanachnu oseqim biqriat shema utepilla o bedibre tora tzarik lihyot hammachaneh qadosh, shello tehe tzoa megulleh sham, velo yihyeh debar erva keneged panayv shel adam beet sheqqore battora o mebarek umitpallel, mippene sheiqqar machanehu shel adam hu keneged panayv vetzarik sheyyihyeh machaneh zeh qadosh veissur zeh hu min hattora, vehachakamim hosipu shehammeqomot asher shoken Adonai biqrabenu shehem rosho shel adam sheshsham hammocha sheshsham hammachashaba, velibbo shel adam shahu hakkavvana, tzarik gam ken shello yihyu roin et haerva beet sheqqore, ella yihyeh hepseq vachatzitza ben rosho velibbo uben haerva, lepikak im eno labush miknasayim o ezor nimtza libbo roeh et haerva veasur liqrot o lebarek veyesh mi sheoser bikhay gavna gam beishsha, vaapillu im yesh lo beged mapsiq ben libbo uben haerva, im kol zeh im haerva megulleh lo yiqra debaenan shettihyeh haerva mekusseh gam meene acherim, dela neemar "lo teraeh" ella "lo yeraeh", lepikak haomed babbayit arom vehotzi rosho lachallon shello yireh ervato ap al pi shekkissa libbo bebeged hare zeh al yiqra mippene sheervato megulleh babbayit, abal im yosheb arom bekilla sheen bah gobah asara tepachim vehotzi rosho chutz lakkilla, vegam kissa bebeged al libbo ap al pi sheervato megulleh bekilla hare zeh kimkussah mippene sheen bah gobah asara tepachim vela dame lebayit shehu chaluq reshut leatzmo vekevan deniret haerva betoko asur veayyen lehaggaon rabbenu zalman beshulchan aruk:

clarification.explanation: The Torah states, "For the Lord your God walks in the midst of your camp... therefore your camp shall be holy, that He see no unseemly thing in you," and the Sages learned from this that it is a positive commandment: whenever we are engaged in sanctity — such as the recitation of the Shema, prayer, or words of Torah — the camp must be holy. That is, there must be no exposed excrement in the place, and no nakedness before a person's face while he recites, blesses, or prays, since a person's essential "camp" is that which is before his face. This prohibition is from the Torah. The Sages added that the places where the Lord dwells within us — namely the head, where the brain and thought are, and the heart, where intention is — must also not face nakedness. Therefore there must be a separation between the head and heart and the nakedness. Hence one who does not wear trousers or a belt has his heart facing his nakedness, and it is forbidden for him to recite or bless — and some forbid this even regarding a woman. And even if there is a garment separating the heart from the nakedness, if the nakedness itself is exposed it is forbidden to recite, since it must be covered also from the eyes of others, as it is said "it shall not be seen" and not "you shall not see." Therefore one standing naked in a house who puts his head out a window so that his own nakedness will not be seen, even though he covered his heart with a garment, may not recite, since his nakedness is exposed within the house. But one sitting naked inside a canopy whose height is less than ten handbreadths, who puts his head outside the canopy and covers his heart, is considered covered, since the canopy is not a domain unto itself like a house.
takeaways: During the recitation of the Shema, prayer, blessings, and words of Torah, the place must, by Torah law, be free of excrement and of nakedness
A separation is required between the heart and the nakedness; therefore without trousers or a belt it is forbidden to recite or bless
The nakedness must be covered also from the eyes of others, not merely such that the person himself does not see it

paragraphs: Mayim apillu hem tzillulin chashibi kissuy laerva ubilbad sheyyotze rosho velibbo chutz lammayim shello yihyeh libbo im ervato tachat mikseh echad, veim libbo tok hammayim asur mishshum libbo roeh et haerva veim hammayim akurim en ebarayv nirin bahem muttar dachashibi hepseq ben libbo laerva umuttar liqrot o lebarek betokam, vehakkesuy shemmekasseh beyado eno chashub kissuy dehalleb vehayyad gup echad hem, al ken im rosho megulleh deasur lo lebarek begilluy harosh, la mehanne leh lekassot rosho beyadayv kede lebarek. mihu ap al gab deyadayv la chashiba kissuy chashiba hepseq, lepikak im mechabbeq gupo bizrootayv chashib zeh hepseq ben leb laerva veayyen shulchan aruk lerabbenu zalman:

clarification.explanation: Water is considered a covering for the nakedness, even if it is clear, provided that his head and heart are outside the water, so that the heart and the nakedness not be together under one covering. If his heart is within the water, it is forbidden, because his heart faces the nakedness. And if the water is murky, such that his limbs are not visible in it, it is permitted to recite and bless within it even if his heart is in the water, since the murky water separates between the heart and the nakedness. The covering that a person covers with his hand is not considered a covering, since the hand and the heart are one body. Therefore one whose head is exposed, for whom it is forbidden to bless with an exposed head, cannot cover his head with his hands in order to bless. And although the hand is not considered a covering, it is considered a separation; therefore if he embraces his body with his arms, this is considered a separation between the heart and the nakedness, and it is permitted.
takeaways: Water, even clear water, is considered a covering for the nakedness on condition that the head and heart are outside the water
Murky water separates between the heart and the nakedness and permits reciting even when the heart is within it
The hand is not considered a covering but is considered a separation, so embracing one's arms around the body separates between the heart and the nakedness

paragraphs: Ap al gab dishar ebarayv im roin et haerva muttar liqrot mikkol maqom im ezeh meebarayv nogea beervato o beervat chabero asur liqrot o lehitpallel, velaken tzarik lehizzaher shello yihyeh nogea haggid beyarkotayv beli hepseq beged benehem, abal al hakkis shel habbetzim en lachush im nogea beyarkotayv ap al pi degam keneged hakkis asur liqrot belo kissuy mishshum d"l yeraeh beka vego'":

clarification.explanation: Although it is permitted to recite when one's other limbs face the nakedness, nevertheless if one of his limbs touches his own nakedness or another's nakedness, it is forbidden to recite or pray. Therefore one must be careful that the membrum not touch the thighs without a garment separating between them. But regarding the scrotum there is no concern if it touches the thighs, even though facing the scrotum it is also forbidden to recite without a covering, because of "and He shall not see in you an unseemly thing."
takeaways: A limb touching nakedness, one's own or another's, forbids reciting and praying
A garment must separate between the membrum and the thighs
The scrotum touching the thighs does not prevent reciting, but it still requires a covering when facing it

paragraphs: Im haya lobesh hammiknasayim lebad dachatzi hattachton shello mekusseh, vegam yesh hepseq ben libbo laerva veraq chatzi haelyon megulleh sheeno lobesh chaluq muttar liqrot qeriat shema, abal lehitpallel asur debitpilla tzarik lirot atzmo keomed lipne hammelek shetztzarik laamod beema:

clarification.explanation: One who wears only trousers, such that his lower half is covered and there is a separation between his heart and the nakedness, and only his upper half is exposed because he is not wearing a shirt, is permitted to recite the Shema. But to pray is forbidden, because in prayer a person must regard himself as standing before the King, and he must stand in awe and gravity.
takeaways: With the upper half of the body exposed, when the nakedness is covered and there is a separation to the heart, it is permitted to recite the Shema
Praying with the body half exposed is forbidden
In prayer one must stand in awe, as one standing before the King

paragraphs: Asur liqrot keneged ervat chabero veissur zeh hu min hattora, abal ervat behema muttar liqrot kenegdah, veervat akku"m gam ken asur liqrot kenegdah, veyesh oserin liqrot keneged ervat qatan apillu ben yomo, dela hittiru ella bishat hammila, veap al pi deyesh mattirin, tzarik lachush lisbarat haoserin, velo yiqra keneged ervat qatan apillu ben yomo vekannizkar baacharonim:

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to recite facing another person's nakedness, and this prohibition is from the Torah. But it is permitted to recite facing the nakedness of an animal. The nakedness of a gentile is likewise forbidden to recite facing. And some forbid reciting facing the nakedness of a minor, even one a day old, since it was permitted only at the time of circumcision. And although there are those who permit it, it is proper to be concerned for the opinion of those who forbid it, and not to recite facing the nakedness of a minor even one a day old.
takeaways: It is forbidden by Torah law to recite facing a person's nakedness, including that of a gentile
The nakedness of an animal is permitted
It is proper to be stringent and not recite even facing the nakedness of a day-old infant

paragraphs: Hayeta erva kenegdo vehechezir panayv mimmenna im kol gupo ad shennaaset meachorayv o min hatztzad muttar liqrot veap al pi shehu samuk lah, ki beerva biriyya tala hakkatub dela asur ella erva hanniret, mihu im haerva kenegdo veetzem eno, o shehu suma, o ballayla bachoshek vaapela sheen roeh otah asur liqrot, dela neemar "lo tireh" ella amar "lo yeraeh", veim roeh et haerva derek ashashit shebbachallon apillu hi bebayit acher shehu reshut acher asur liqrot, debiriyya tala hakkatub vahare hi niret lepanayv:

clarification.explanation: If nakedness was facing him and he turned his face and his whole body away from it, until it came to be behind him or to the side, it is permitted to recite even though he is adjacent to it, since the Torah made the prohibition dependent on seeing, and only nakedness that is visible is forbidden. But if the nakedness is facing him and he closes his eyes, or he is blind, or it is a dark night and he does not see it, it is forbidden to recite, as it is said "it shall not be seen" and not "you shall not see" — that is, the prohibition does not depend on his own act of seeing but on the fact that it is in a state of being visible. And if he sees the nakedness through glass in a window, even if it is in another house and another domain, it is forbidden to recite, since it is indeed visible before him.
takeaways: Turning the whole body away from the nakedness permits reciting even while adjacent to it
Closing one's eyes, blindness, or darkness do not permit it, since the prohibition does not depend on one's own act of seeing
Nakedness visible through glass is forbidden even though it is in another domain

paragraphs: Muttar leharher bedibre tora keshehu arom, vaapillu keneged erva acheret gam ken muttar leharher shenneemar "ervat dabar", dibbur asur hirhur muttar, umikkol maqom asur lishmoa beraka mechabero shehu tzarik latzet bishmia zo yede chobato, deek nomar shomea keoneh vahare hu arom deeno yakol laanot vekannizkar beshulchan aruk lerabbenu zalman, velaken haholekim litbila umeharharim ezeh kavvanot bishat tebila muttar, ubilbad shello yotziu mippihem ezeh pasuq o debar tora meachar shehem arumim, abal vidduy yukal lehitvaddot sham beodo arom bammiqveh apillu dehammayim tzelulim velibbo hu tok hammayim shehu im ervato bemikseh echad:

clarification.explanation: It is permitted to contemplate words of Torah while naked, and even facing another's nakedness it is permitted to contemplate, since it is said "an unseemly matter" — speech is forbidden but contemplation is permitted. Nevertheless it is forbidden to hear a blessing from another while naked if he needs to fulfill his obligation through this hearing, since the rule of "one who hears is as one who answers" means it is considered as though he himself answered — and how can he answer while naked? Therefore those who go to immerse and contemplate intentions during the immersion, it is permitted, provided they do not utter with their mouths any verse or word of Torah while naked. But he may recite confession there while still naked in the mikveh, even when the water is clear and his heart is within the water together with his nakedness under a single covering.
takeaways: Contemplating words of Torah is permitted even while naked and even facing nakedness
One may not fulfill the obligation of a blessing by hearing it from another while naked, since he cannot answer
Confession may be recited in the mikveh even while still naked

paragraphs: Tepach megulleh beishsha bemaqom sheddarkah lekassot hare zo erva, veasur liqrot kenegdo qeriat shema vekol dabar shebbiqdushsha, vaapillu hi ishto, abal happanim vehayyadayim sheddarkan lihyot megullin muttar liqrot kenegdan apillu beishsha acheret, veyesh omerim dela ameru tepach beishsha erva ella davqa beishto, abal beishsha acheret apillu pachot mittepach have erva bekol maqom sheddarkah lekassot veyesh lachush ledibrehem, ubi"chesed laalapim" za"l nistappeq im gam biqtanna yesh lachush letappeach megulleh bemaqom shedderek lekassot ayyen sham, ubesipri haqqatan "mqbtzyl" katabti deyesh lehachmir gam biqtanna heka deepshar, uneshe haarbiyyim sheddarkam legallot zerootehem ap al pi sheddarkam tamid bekak lo yiqra kenegdam:

clarification.explanation: A handbreadth of exposure on a woman, in a place she customarily covers, is considered nakedness, and it is forbidden to recite the Shema and anything of sanctity facing it, even if she is his wife. But the face and hands, which are customarily exposed, may be faced in reciting even regarding another woman. And some say that the rule of "a handbreadth on a woman is nakedness" was said only regarding his own wife, but regarding another woman even less than a handbreadth is considered nakedness in any place she customarily covers, and one should be concerned for their words. And regarding a minor girl, one should be stringent where possible. And regarding Arab women whose custom is to expose their arms, even though this is always their custom, one should not recite facing them.
takeaways: A handbreadth of exposure on a woman, in a place she customarily covers, is considered nakedness, even in the case of one's own wife
The face and hands, which are customarily exposed, are permitted
Regarding another woman one should be stringent even for less than a handbreadth, and likewise regarding a minor girl

paragraphs: Yesh mi sheoser gam leishsha liqrot o lehitpallel keneged ishsha acheret aruma, mihu kol zeh davqa baaruma, abal keneged tepach megulleh bemaqom shedderek lekassoto bipne haanashim, en bazeh issur leishsha keneged ishsha acheret:

clarification.explanation: There is one who forbids also a woman from reciting or praying facing another woman who is naked. But all this applies specifically when she is actually naked; but facing a handbreadth exposed in a place customarily covered before men, there is no prohibition in this for a woman facing another woman.
takeaways: A woman is forbidden to recite facing another woman who is fully naked
A handbreadth of exposure on a woman does not forbid another woman from reciting facing her

paragraphs: Ishsha shemmeniqa et benah umegalla daddeha, asur liqrot o lebarek kenegdah, apillu hi ishto vekol shekken beishsha acheret, veyesh omerim dekevan dehaishsha darkah legallot daddeha bizman hayyeniqa hare haddaddim nechshabim oto zeman kemo kappot hayyadayim vehappanim, veraq im enah meniqa sheddarkah lehatznia daddeha umaqpedet al zeh az asur liqrot kenegdah, veyesh lismok al sebara zo bishat haddechaq:

clarification.explanation: A woman who is nursing her son and exposes her breasts — it is forbidden to recite or bless facing her, even if she is his wife, and all the more so regarding another woman. And some say that since it is a woman's custom to expose her breasts at the time of nursing, the breasts are then considered like the palms of the hands and the face, and only if she is not nursing — when her custom is to conceal her breasts and she is particular about this — is it forbidden to recite facing her. And one may rely on this reasoning in a time of pressing need.
takeaways: Facing a nursing woman whose breasts are exposed, it is forbidden to recite and bless
In a time of pressing need there are those who are lenient during the time of nursing, since that is then her custom

paragraphs: Ap al gab dibaddara rabba ita vezeh leshono (zohar cheleq g qmb, ): qol beishsha erva, sear beishsha erva shoq beishsha erva, regel beishsha erva, yd beishsha erva, veap al gab ditren illen la shennivva chabrana, teren illen yattir meerva innun ad kan leshono, hinneh ayyen lerabbenu haari"y za"l beshaar maamre rashbi"y[1] mah shekkatab bebeur maamar hannizkar, ubesipri haqqatan "mqbtzyl" katabti besiyyata dishmayya degam ledibre zohar haqqadosh hannizkarim hacheleq min hayyad umin haregel sheddarko lihyot megulleh kegon hakkap vehaetzbaot muttar liqrot kenegdam deen niqra al zeh shem erva:

clarification.explanation: Although the Zohar (Idra Rabba) states, "A voice in a woman is nakedness, hair in a woman is nakedness, a leg in a woman is nakedness, a foot in a woman is nakedness, a hand in a woman is nakedness," and although these two, the hand and the foot, are more than nakedness, nevertheless Rabbenu the Ari explained this statement, and the Ben Ish Chai wrote in his book "Makabtziel" that also according to the Zohar, the part of the hand and the foot that is customarily exposed, such as the palm of the hand and the fingers, it is permitted to recite facing them, since this is not called by the name of nakedness.
takeaways: The words of the Zohar regarding a woman's hand and foot as nakedness are explained as referring to the parts that are customarily covered
The palm of the hand and the fingers, which are customarily exposed, are not nakedness and it is permitted to recite facing them

paragraphs: Sear shel ishsha sheddarkah lekassoto erva hi, veasur liqrot ulehitpallel ulebarek kenegdo vaapillu bisar ishto, veen chilluq bazeh ben ishsha keura uzeqena vekayyotze, abal betulot sheddarkan lelek peruot rosh, veken searot shel nashim shergilin latzet chutz letzammatan biqtzat aratzot muttar liqrot kenegdan kevan sheddarkan bekak uregilin bahem, veken nashim sheddarkan laasot sear rosham qeliot mishtalshelin laachorehem kevan sheddarkan bekak muttar liqrot kenegdan, ubesipri haqqatan "mqbtzyl" haaleti dehannashim beare eroppa sheddarkan lelek tamid perue rosh muttar liqrot kenegdan, kevan dekol hannashim darkan bekak, mihu sham beare eroppa darkam shel nashim labush anniplaot tamid veen nireh apillu kelal dehu mikkappot raglehem, hinneh orach haholek sham ap al pi sheishto enah noheget bekak ki bimqomah darkan shel nashim lelek bekappot raglehem begilluy, hinneh hu tzarik lehizzaher sham bazeh lachshob kappot haraglayim kullam mimmeqomot hamkussim kepi minhag bammaqom hahu veasur liqrot kenegdan:

clarification.explanation: The hair of a woman that she customarily covers is nakedness, and it is forbidden to recite, pray, and bless facing it, even the hair of one's own wife, and there is no distinction in this between an ugly woman or an old woman. But unmarried maidens, who customarily go with heads uncovered, and likewise hair that customarily emerges beyond the braid in certain lands, it is permitted to recite facing them, since that is their custom. And likewise women who make their hair into braids that hang down behind them, since that is their custom, it is permitted to recite facing them. And regarding women in the cities of Europe, whose custom is to always go with heads uncovered, it is permitted to recite facing them, since it is the custom of all women there. However, in those places the custom of women is to always wear stockings, such that nothing at all of the soles of their feet is visible; therefore a traveler who goes there, even though his own wife does not follow that custom, must be careful there to consider the soles of the feet entirely as covered places according to the custom of that locale, and it is forbidden to recite facing them.
takeaways: A woman's hair, which she customarily covers, is nakedness, even the hair of one's own wife
Where hair is customarily exposed, such as with unmarried maidens or by local custom, there is no prohibition
The law depends on local custom, so in a place where a particular part is customarily covered, it is considered nakedness there

paragraphs: Qol zemer shel ishsha ben penuya ben eshet ish, vaapillu qol zemer shel ishto hu erva veasur liqrot bedibre tora o lehitpallel ulebarek kesheshshomeo, veen chilluq bazeh ben keura o zeqena, upoh irenu derek hannashim lihyot poot letinoq habbokeh beqol niggun beazenayv kede lehashtiqo ulehabi lo hashshena, vetzarik lizzaher shello yilmad beet shehaishsha poa umenaggenet letinoq vaapillu hi ishto, mihu bat qetanna pachot mishshesh shanim en lachush im poa umenaggenet letinoq, veod gam ken darkam poh irenu y" lehabi etzel hakkalla ballayla sheqqodem hachuppa nashim menaggenot, sheasur leadam lilmod bedibre tora im shomea qolam veim i epshar lo sheyyelek lemaqom acher yilmad al yede hirhur shemmeayyen basseper velo yotzi bispatayv kelum demuttar bikhay gavna bishat haddechaq, veyesh machmirim apillu bimdabberet im hi medabber debarim arukkim shel sippure maasiyyot vekayyotze, abal debarim qetzarim ubiprat shehem letzorek eseq en lachush:

clarification.explanation: The singing voice of a woman, whether unmarried or married, and even the singing voice of one's own wife, is considered nakedness, and it is forbidden to recite words of Torah, to pray, and to bless while hearing it, and there is no distinction between an ugly woman or an old woman. In the place of the Ben Ish Chai, it is the custom of women to hum a melodic sound to a crying infant in order to quiet it and put it to sleep, and one must be careful not to study while the woman is humming and singing to the infant, even if she is his own wife. But regarding a small girl under six years old, there is no concern. And likewise it is their custom to bring singing women to the bride on the night before the wedding, and it is forbidden to study Torah while hearing their voices; and if it is not possible to go elsewhere, he should study by contemplation alone, examining a book, without uttering anything with his lips, which is permitted in a time of pressing need. Some are stringent even regarding a woman's speech when she speaks lengthy matters, but regarding brief matters, particularly for the sake of business, there is no concern.
takeaways: A woman's singing voice is nakedness, and it is forbidden to study, pray, and bless while hearing it
In a time of pressing need when one cannot move away, one should study by contemplation from the book without speaking
Ordinary and brief speech by a woman, particularly for a purpose, is not forbidden

paragraphs: Asur liqrot min hattora kol debar qedushsha keneged hatztzoa shel adam, veim hayeta meachorayv o mitztziddo yirchaq mimmenna arba ammot veqore veim lepanayv yitracheq melo enayv sheyyitracheq beopen shello yukal lirotah, uballayla yeshaer keshiur hayyom vehassuma meshaer kepi reiyyat happiqqeach, utzedadim shellepanayv hare hem kilpanayv, veshelleacharayv hare hem kilacharayv, veim betziddo veroeh otah belo hattayat rosho latztzedadin hare zeh kilpanayv, vetzarik kimlo enayv: veha desaggi bearba ammot, haynu heka deen maggia lo recha mimmenna, abal im maggia lo recha ra mimmenna tzarik sheyyitracheq arba ammot mimmaqom shekkala harecha, vaapillu im zeh haqqore yesh lo choli hazzikma (nazzelet) sheeno mericha, tzarik sheyyitracheq arba ammot mimmaqom shekkala harecha lishar adam shemmericha vehashshiur hu beadam benoni, ki yesh bene adam shechush harecha shellahem chazaq meod shemmerichim merachoq yoter:

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to recite anything of sanctity facing a person's excrement. If it is behind him or to his side, he should distance himself four cubits from it and recite. If it is before him, he should distance himself the full extent of his eyes, to a place where he cannot see it. At night he estimates as by the measure of the day, and a blind person estimates according to the sight of one who can see. Sides before him are considered as before him, and those behind him as behind him, and if it is to his side and he sees it without turning his head, it is considered as before him. The distance of four cubits suffices only where no odor reaches him from it, but if a bad odor reaches him, he must distance himself four cubits from the place where the odor ends. And even one who cannot smell due to congestion must distance himself four cubits from the place where the odor ends for an ordinary person who can smell, following the measure of an average person.
takeaways: Facing excrement, one distances four cubits if it is behind or to the side, or the full extent of one's eyes if it is in front
The distance of four cubits helps only where no bad odor reaches him; where it does, he must distance himself to where the odor ends
The measure is judged by an average person's sense of smell, not by one who cannot smell or one with an unusually strong sense of smell

paragraphs: Hayeta hatztzoa bemaqom gabohha asara tepachim verachab arbaa tepachim al arbaa tepachim, hare zeh reshut leatzmo, vekol sheeno maggia lo recha ra mimmenna muttar liqrot ap al pi sheroeh otah, veyesh omerim apillu hatztzoa birshut acher gabohha asara, o miqqop mechitztzot, o bebayit acher kol shehu roeh otah asur liqrot, veyesh lachush ledibrehem lehachmir beshel tora, mihu im meetzim enayv o shehu ballayla, yesh lehaqel im hi birshut acher:

clarification.explanation: If the excrement was in a place ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths by four handbreadths wide, it is a domain unto itself, and wherever no bad odor reaches him, it is permitted to recite even though he sees it. And some say that even excrement in another domain that is ten handbreadths high, or surrounded by partitions, or in another house, wherever he sees it, it is forbidden to recite, and one should be concerned for their words so as to be stringent in a Torah matter. However, if he closes his eyes, or it is nighttime, one may be lenient if it is in another domain.
takeaways: Excrement in a place ten handbreadths high and four wide is considered a domain unto itself, and it is permitted to recite if there is no odor
Some are stringent to forbid any visible excrement even in another domain
With closed eyes or at night one may be lenient when it is in another domain

paragraphs: Recha ra eno moil lo mechitztza veshinnuy reshut, sheapillu hasserachon munnach achar shelosha vearbaa battim im maggia lo recha asur liqrot, veraq mi sheyyesh lo choli hazzikma (nazzelet) sheeno mericha kevan dehasserachon eno babbayit sheomed bo muttar liqrot ap al pi daacherim merichim, veraq im hi beoto habbayit az gam baal choli hazzekama asur liqrot kol od daacherim haomedim sham merichim recha ra, veken im hayeta tzoa babbayit vehesiro otah mishsham, vaadayin yesh recha ra asur liqrot ad sheyyikleh harecha, abal im hu baal choli sheeno mericha shari leh liqrot achar shehesiru veheebiru hatztzoa min habbayit:

clarification.explanation: A bad odor is not exempted by a partition or a change of domain, and even if the stench lies three or four houses away, as long as the odor reaches him it is forbidden to recite. Only one who cannot smell due to congestion, since the stench is not in the house in which he stands, is permitted to recite even though others do smell it. But if the excrement is in that same house, even the one with congestion is forbidden to recite as long as others standing there smell a bad odor. And likewise if there was excrement in a house and it was removed, and a bad odor still remains, it is forbidden to recite until the odor ends, but one who cannot smell is permitted to recite after the excrement has been removed from the house.
takeaways: A bad odor forbids even through a partition or another domain as long as it reaches him
One who cannot smell is permitted when the stench is not in the house he stands in
Even after the excrement is removed it remains forbidden until the odor ends, for one who can smell

paragraphs: Nebela musrachat vekol dabar hammusrach mechamat shennitappesh, veken ashpa sherechah ra umayim seruchin shebbarechobot, kol ellu asur min hattora liqrot kenegdam, veyitracheq mehem kedin tzoat adam:

clarification.explanation: A stinking carcass and anything that has stunk from decay, and likewise refuse that smells bad and foul water in the streets — all these it is forbidden by Torah law to recite facing, and one should distance oneself from them as with the law of human excrement.
takeaways: A stinking carcass, refuse, and foul water are governed by the same law as human excrement
The prohibition against reciting facing them is from the Torah
One distances from them as with the law of human excrement

paragraphs: Tzoat behema chayya veop im yesh bahem recha ra hare hem ketzoat adam, veim en bahem recha ra muttar liqrot kenegdam, ak rob tzoat behema chayya veop en bahem recha ra, vetzoat keleb o chazir im natan bahem orot marchiqin mehem ketzoat adam abal tzoat chatul vetzoa rakka shel chamor habba min hadderek setaman rechan ra ketzoat adam, velaken apillu im yizdammen paam achat sheen lahem recha ra apillu hake asur liqrot kenegdam, veyitracheq mehem kedin tzoat adam, veken tzoat tarnegolim adummim setaman rechan ra vetzarik lehitracheq mehem ketzoat adam, abal tzoat shear tarnegolim dinam ketzoat shear opot, vehillul shel tarnegolim yesh bo serachon vedino ketzoat adam vehu haddin ledir behemot sherecho ra:

clarification.explanation: The excrement of a domesticated animal, a wild animal, or a fowl, if it has a bad odor, is governed like human excrement, and if it has no bad odor, it is permitted to recite facing it, and most such excrement has no bad odor. The excrement of a dog or pig, if hides were tanned with it, one distances from it as with human excrement. The excrement of a cat, and the soft excrement of a donkey coming from the road, generally has a bad odor like human excrement, and therefore even if on one occasion it has no odor, it is forbidden to recite facing it and one must distance from it. The excrement of red chickens generally has a bad odor and one must distance from it like human excrement, but that of other chickens follows the law of other fowl. A chicken coop has a stench and its law is like human excrement, and likewise an animal pen whose odor is bad.
takeaways: The excrement of domesticated animals, wild animals, and fowl depends on odor, and most of it has no bad odor
The excrement of cats, of a donkey coming from the road, and of red chickens has a bad odor like human excrement
A chicken coop and an animal pen whose odor is bad are governed like human excrement

paragraphs: Me raglayim shel adam beshaa shemmashtin asur liqrot kenegdan min hattora abal leachar shennapelu laaretz o bikli asur midderabbanan, velaken kevan deissuram midderabbanan heqellu bahem veameru deim achar shehishtin keli hetil letoko rebiit mayim hare zeh muttar liqrot kenegdam, veken hu haddin im haya bikli meiqqara rebiit mayim vehishtin betoko demuttar, veshiur zeh dirbiit ben im hishtin harbeh ben im hishtin meat vaapillu tippa achat dela pelug rabbanan, ulekak im hishtin bikli veheriqu hahashtana bemaqom acher, asur liqrot keneged oto keli im lo yattil letoko rebiit mayim, daapillu dehuraq i epshar shello yishshaer bo lichlucha shel me raglayim meat shehu topeach al menat lehatpicha, mihu rebiit zo la mehanne ella lehashtana achat, abal shette hishtannut tzarik lahem shette rebiiyyot, uleshalosh tzarik shalosh veken al zeh hadderek leolam veim niblea hahashtana babbeged o baqqarqa, veen belichlucha topeach al menat lehatpicha muttar liqrot kenegdam:

clarification.explanation: Human urine, at the time a person is urinating, it is forbidden by Torah law to recite facing it, but after it has fallen to the ground or into a vessel, it is forbidden only by rabbinic law. And since its prohibition is rabbinic, they were lenient: if after urinating he cast a quarter-log of water into the vessel, it is permitted to recite facing it, and likewise if there was originally a quarter-log of water in the vessel and he urinated into it. This measure of a quarter-log is required whether he urinated much or little, even a single drop, since the Sages did not distinguish. If he urinated into a vessel and poured the urine out elsewhere, it is forbidden to recite facing the vessel unless he casts a quarter-log of water into it, since some moisture sufficient to moisten upon contact necessarily remains. A single quarter-log avails only for one act of urination; for two acts, two quarter-logs are needed, and so on. And if the urine was absorbed into a garment or the ground, and there is no moisture sufficient to moisten upon contact, it is permitted to recite facing them.
takeaways: Urine at the time of urinating is forbidden by Torah law, and after falling into a vessel or onto the ground it is forbidden only rabbinically
Casting a quarter-log of water for each act of urination permits reciting facing the vessel
Urine that has been absorbed and leaves no moisture sufficient to moisten upon contact is permitted

paragraphs: Abit shel me raglayim shehu hakkeli shemmashtinim bo tamid, veken gerap shel rei im hem shel cheres o etz apillu rechutzim yapeh veen bahem recha ra, vaapillu kepan al pihem dinan ketzoa, vela mehanne hattalat rebiit mayim o yoter, abal shel matteket o zekukit o cheres metzuppeh eber urechutzim yapeh yapeh mibbachutz umibbipnim, veen lahem recha ra muttar liqrot kenegdo veen tzarik lahem kepiyya al pihem:

clarification.explanation: A chamber pot for urine, the vessel one regularly urinates into, and likewise a pot for excrement, if they are of earthenware or wood, even if washed well and having no bad odor, and even if turned upside down on their opening, are governed like excrement, and casting in a quarter-log of water or more does not help. But if they are of metal, glass, or earthenware coated with tin, and washed very well both outside and inside, and have no bad odor, it is permitted to recite facing them, and there is no need even to turn them upside down.
takeaways: A chamber pot and a waste pot of earthenware or wood are governed like excrement even when clean
Such vessels of metal, glass, or coated earthenware, when clean and odorless, may be faced while reciting
For the permitted vessels there is no need even to turn them upside down

paragraphs: Im beshaa shehu mebarek o qore hirgish shennitlakleku hammiknasayim shello behishtanna shari, ap al pi shehem topeach al menat lehatpicha mippene shehem mekussim babbeged haelyon:

clarification.explanation: If, while he is blessing or reciting, he notices that his trousers have become soiled with urine, it is permitted for him to continue, even though they carry moisture sufficient to moisten upon contact, since they are covered by the outer garment.
takeaways: Trousers soiled with urine that are covered by an outer garment do not forbid reciting
The covering of the outer garment permits it even when there is moisture sufficient to moisten upon contact

paragraphs: Kol maqom sherauy listappaq bo im yesh bo tzoa o lav asur liqrot qeriat shema vekol dabar shebbiqdushsha ad sheyyibdoq hammaqom veim eno yakol libdoq mippene shehu ballayla o sibba acheret hare zeh asur liqrot dehave sepeq tora bammeh debarim amurim betzoa sheissurah hu min hattora, abal me raglayim muttar, deen issuran min hattora ella keneged ammud shel qillucha, laken im hem betok keli veeno yodea im hem hishtanna o shear mayim, kevan deeno yakol libdoq hare zeh qore missapeq, dezeh have sepeqa derabbanan velo aseru ella bevaddaan velo bispeqan, veim matza tzoa beezeh maqom veeno yodea im hi shel adam o shel kelabim, tolin bammatzuy deim metzuyyan beoto maqom tinoqot yoter mikkelabim tolin betinoqot veasur, veim metzuyim kelabim yoter tolin biklabim: veim qara qeriat shema o hitpallel bemaqom sheen rauy lehistappeq bo sheyyesh bo tzoa, veachar kak matza bo en tzarik lachazor ulehitpallel, abal chozer veqore qeriat shema belo berakot, abal im qara qeriat shema o hitpallel bemaqom sherauy lehistappeq bo betzoa, vehu lo badaq mittechilla veachar kak matza sham tzoa tzarik lachazor ulehitpallel veal zeh neemar "zebach reshaim toeba" (mishle k, kz), vekol shekken im yada sheyyesh tzoa veqara vehitpallel bemezid, bammeh debarim amurim betzoa abal beme raglayim apillu qara qeriat shema vehitpallel bemaqom sherauy lehistappeq bahem veachar kak nimtza sham, en tzarik lachazor liqrot hoil veen issuran ella middibre soperim vetzarik lehashgicha heteb beinyanim kaelleh kol adam bechatzrotayv vetirotayv bemaqom shedderek haqqetannim letannep bo, gam poh irenu al sepat hannahar chiddeqel hen tok hair hen chutz lair, shekicha umatzuy sham tzoat adam min oberim veshabim ubiprat sepat hannahar shellipne hakkeramim, dekol otam baale hakkeramim darkam lippanot al sepat hannahar, deen leadam lehitpallel al sepat hannahar ad sheyyibdoq, veken tzarik lehashgicha kesheholek barechobot umeboot shebbair shello ledabber bedibre tora im chabero ad sheyyireh im hammaqom naqi, ki poh irenu yesh kamma bene adam oberim veshabim sheosim tzarekehem ballayla betok hammeboot urechobot shel hair, velipamim gam bayyom osim ki en ish sam al leb ledabar zeh poh irenu, umeporash bedibre rabbenu haari"y za"l bezeh hallashon: issur hazkarat dibre tora bimboot hamtunnapot gorem lehaknis qodesh bechol ad kan leshono, veayyen beshaar maamre rashbi"y dap sb ammud g:

clarification.explanation: Any place where there is room to doubt whether there is excrement in it, it is forbidden to recite the Shema and anything of sanctity until the place is examined, and if he cannot examine it, because it is nighttime or for some other reason, it is forbidden to recite, since this is a doubt in a matter whose prohibition is from the Torah. But regarding urine it is permitted, since its prohibition is not from the Torah except facing the actual stream, and therefore if it is in a vessel and he does not know whether it is urine or other water, he recites out of doubt, since this is a rabbinic doubt and they forbade it only when certain. If he found excrement and does not know whether it is human or of dogs, one follows the majority, and if infants are more commonly found in that place than dogs, one follows the assumption of infants and it is forbidden. If he recited or prayed in a place where there was no reasonable doubt and afterward found excrement, he need not repeat the prayer, but he does repeat the recitation of the Shema without the blessings. But if he recited or prayed in a place where there was reasonable room for doubt and he did not examine it, and afterward found excrement, he must repeat the prayer, of which it is said, "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination." Regarding urine, one need not repeat even if it is later found, since its prohibition is only from the words of the Scribes. And a person must supervise carefully his courtyards and places where children are accustomed to soil, and in the place of the Ben Ish Chai, on the bank of the Tigris river, human excrement is commonly found, and therefore one should not pray there until he examines it, and likewise one should be careful when walking in the streets and lanes of the city not to speak words of Torah until he sees that the place is clean. And Rabbenu the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote of this in severe language: the prohibition against mentioning words of Torah in soiled lanes causes the bringing of the holy into the profane — that is, one who is not careful and mentions matters of sanctity in such unclean places thereby causes the mixing and bringing of sanctity into impurity and the profane, and therefore one must be very careful about this and not take it lightly.
takeaways: In a doubt regarding excrement it is forbidden to recite until examined, and if examination is impossible it is forbidden, as a doubt in a matter of Torah law
In a doubt regarding urine it is permitted, as a rabbinic doubt
One who prayed in a place with reasonable room for doubt and did not examine it, and excrement was then found, must repeat the prayer

Rabbenu the Ari warned that mentioning words of Torah in soiled lanes causes 'bringing the holy into the profane' — a spiritual flaw of mixing sanctity and impurity, not merely a technical prohibition

paragraphs: Qatan sheyyakol leekol kazzayit dagan bikde akilat peras, apillu sheeno yakol leakelo ella al yede bishshul kegon daysa vekayyotze, hare bene meayim shello bevadday masrechin kol mine maakol sheyyokal, vetzarik lehitracheq mitztzoato kekimmu tzoat gadol, vekol zeh min din abal lekattechilla tob lehitracheq apillu mitztzoat qatan ben yomo veken nohagim:

clarification.explanation: A minor who is able to eat an olive's-bulk of grain within the time it takes to eat a half-loaf, even if he can eat it only cooked, as in porridge, his intestines already cause any food he eats to putrefy, and one must distance oneself from his excrement just as from that of an adult. This is by strict law, but as an initial preference it is good to distance oneself even from the excrement of a minor a day old, and so is the custom.
takeaways: A minor who eats an olive's-bulk of grain has excrement like that of an adult, from which one distances
As an initial preference it is good to distance oneself even from the excrement of a day-old infant
So is the custom

paragraphs: Tzoa apillu yebesha veen bah recha asur liqrot kenegdah abal yebesha kol kak ad shettitparek al yede gelila haveya keapar, umuttar liqrot kenegdah im higgia yobesh shellah leshiur zeh, veim lo titparek al yede gelila ella raq teshabber lishtayim la mehanne liqrot kenegdah:

clarification.explanation: Excrement, even if it is dry and has no odor, it is forbidden to recite facing it. But if it has dried to the point that it crumbles when rolled, it is like dust and it is permitted to recite facing it. But if it does not crumble when rolled but merely breaks in two, this is not sufficient to permit reciting facing it.
takeaways: Dry excrement without odor still forbids reciting
Excrement that has dried to the point of crumbling when rolled is considered like dust and is permitted
Merely breaking in two is not sufficient to permit it

paragraphs: Bet hakkisse shemmuqqap mechitztzot, veyesh lo petach, veasuy bachapira sheharei yored letok hachapira venopel lematta beshippule hammidron, ap al pi sheosim hishtanna al qarqa bet hakkisse muttar liqrot keneged oto bet hakkisse im happetach sagur, velaken tzarik lehizzaher shello lehoshib hayyeladim al qarqa bet hakkisse mippene happachad shemmepachadim lesheb al pi hachapira, deim ken have lah bet hakkisse sheen bo chapira, deaz apillu yesh bo mechitztzot vehappetach sagur asur liqrot kenegdo, ki niddon kol habbet hakkisse kedin gerap shel rei. veim mepachadim hayyeladim yannichu lahem gerap shel rei betok bet hakkisse sheyyaasu tzarekehem bo, gam yesh lehizzaher lipamim shehaggumma titmalle tzoa mechamat shennapal bah eben gedola venistema, veaz hatztzoa maggaat ad sepat hachapira beshetach qarqa bet hakkisse, deen liqrot keneged oto bet hakkisse ad sheyyetaqqenu otah, gam lipamim yesh eben munnachat besop sepat hachapira achore yeshibato shel adam, vezo al harob munnach aleha tzoa mechamat hayyoshebim sheenam yoshebim heteb, tzarik sheyyasimu leb al zot shello yannichu kak, deim ken en qorin keneged oto bet hakkisse apillu happetach sagur veayyen "chesed laalapim" siman pg ot b':

clarification.explanation: A privy surrounded by partitions with a door, built over a pit into which the excrement descends and falls down the slope, even though urination is done on its floor, it is permitted to recite facing it when the door is closed. Therefore one must be careful not to seat children on the floor of the privy out of fear that they will fall into the pit, for if so it becomes a privy without a pit, and then even with partitions and a closed door it is forbidden to recite facing it, since it is treated like a vessel for excrement. If the children are afraid, one should place a pot for excrement for them within the privy. And one must be careful that the hollow not become filled with excrement because a stone fell in and blocked it, such that the excrement reaches the edge of the floor, in which case one may not recite facing it until it is repaired. Likewise if there is a stone at the far edge of the pit behind the seating place, upon which excrement is usually deposited by those who do not sit properly, one must attend to this, for otherwise one may not recite facing it even with the door closed.
takeaways: A privy built over a pit into which the excrement descends is permitted to recite facing when the door is closed
A privy without a pit is treated like a vessel for excrement and is forbidden even with the door closed
Excrement that has become blocked or is deposited at the edge of the pit forbids reciting until it is repaired

paragraphs: Recha ra deen lo iqqar kegon sheyyatza mimmennu rucha millematta, ap al pi demuttar min hattora gazeru chaza"l alayv mishshum recha sheyyesh lo iqqar, velaken asur bedibre tora ubiqriat shema utepilla uberakot ad sheyyikleh harecha mimmennu, bammeh debarim amurim im harucha yatza mimmennu, abal im yatza mechabero muttar bedibre tora dela gazeru chakamim bah mippene bittul bet hammidrash dei epshar lahem lehizzaher bekak, abal biqriat shema utepilla uberakot gazeru apillu berucha hayyotze mechabero, sheyyamtin ad sheyyikleh harecha ra:

clarification.explanation: A bad odor without substance, such as wind emerging from below, although permitted by Torah law, the Sages decreed against it because of an odor that has substance, and therefore it is forbidden during words of Torah, the recitation of the Shema, prayer, and blessings until the odor ends. This applies specifically when the wind emerged from himself, but if it emerged from another, it is permitted for words of Torah, since the Sages did not decree regarding this because of the disruption it would cause to the study hall, it being impossible to be careful about this; but regarding the Shema, prayer, and blessings they decreed even regarding wind emerging from another, that he should wait until the odor ends.
takeaways: Wind emerging from below is forbidden rabbinically for Torah study and prayer until the odor ends
Wind emerging from another person is permitted for words of Torah, because of the disruption to the study hall
For the Shema, prayer, and blessings, one waits even for wind emerging from another

paragraphs: Kol serachon verecha ra shehu mechamat ippush dino ketzoa, abal dabar sherecho ra libne adam lav mechamat ippush ella beriyyato kak kegon nepet, veken mah sheqqorin bearbe qy"r (zepet), ap al gab derechan qasheh en lahem din tzoa veen tzarik lehitracheq mehem, veken hu haddin bekol mine asabim sherechan ra mikkoach tiban uberiyyatam, let lan bah:

clarification.explanation: Any stench or bad odor that comes from decay is governed like excrement. But something whose odor is bad to people not because of decay but because that is its inherent nature, such as petroleum, and likewise pitch, although their odor is harsh, they do not have the law of excrement and there is no need to distance from them. The same applies to all kinds of plants whose odor is bad by their own nature.
takeaways: A bad odor from decay is governed like excrement
Something whose odor is bad by its inherent nature, such as petroleum or pitch, is not like excrement and does not require distancing
The same rule applies to plants whose odor is bad by nature

paragraphs: Im ba lahem recha ra mibbet hakkisse o mibbayit acher beet limmudam bedibre tora, o beet shemmitpallelim, muttar lehashlik beloye sechabot serupim kede sheyyaaleh ashanam veyitbattel harecha ra shello yargishu bo, o yashliku me veradim sheyyesh lahem recha tob vekannizkar baacharonim za"l:

clarification.explanation: If a bad odor comes to them from a privy or another house while they are studying Torah or praying, it is permitted to burn worn-out rags so that the smoke rises and dispels the bad odor so it is not noticed, or to sprinkle rose water, which has a pleasant fragrance.
takeaways: It is permitted to dispel a bad odor coming from outside in order to study and pray
One may raise smoke from burnt rags or use fragrant rose water
